title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer
authors: Debarshi Kundu, Swaroop Ghosh, Vasant G Honavar
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) optimize circuit angles through repeated quantum-device evaluations, often facing vanishing gradients and high optimization costs. We ask whether a large language model (LLM) can write these angles directly. Extending *weight-space programming* from classical networks to quantum circuits, we provide a frontier LLM (\gpt) with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions. Its angles are executed exactly as written, without returning losses, gradients, or accuracy feedback. Across 139 requests, we test handwritten-digit classification, VQE ground-state estimation for spin chains and H$_2$, and MaxCut QAOA, comparing against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit. When parameters have interpretable structure, the LLM matches or approaches the optimizer: it achieves 95--100\% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H$_2$ ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93--96\% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12--18 hand-written weights, outperforming an optimizer trained on the same ten examples. Its weights are also strong warm starts: optimization reaches its best value after a median of one evaluation rather than hundreds. Allowed to design circuits, the LLM chooses data-dependent rotation chains encoding pixel importance in all 30 cases (one qubit for binary tasks, one chain per qubit for ten classes), reaching 65\% accuracy across ten digits. Yet the approach fails in opaque weight spaces: accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, while optimization improves. It is also sensitive to gate conventions: 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail. We release all prompts, replies, and scores.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM can directly write effective variational quantum circuit parameters without optimizer feedback when the parameter space has interpretable structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-written parameters could reduce repeated quantum-device evaluations, either as direct solutions or as strong optimization warm starts.
method: Provide the LLM with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions.
Execute its proposed angles without returning loss, gradient, or accuracy feedback.
Compare against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 139 requests spanning digit classification, VQE, and MaxCut QAOA, LLM weights achieved 93–96% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8, while warm-started optimization reached its best value after a median of one evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability depends on parameter interpretability and gate conventions: fixed classification circuits above 30 weights fell to chance, and 6 of 42 QAOA replies used incorrect mixing-angle signs.
infographic.paper_title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer

title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Bisma Majid, Shabir Ahmad Sofi, Mir Mohammad Yousuf
abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

infographic.key_insight: APGEM adaptively selects error-mitigation techniques from QML training feedback rather than fixing one strategy for the entire experiment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared feedback interface could let engineers reuse one noise-aware controller across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning.
method: Observe fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior at each step.
Use a contextual bandit to select among ZNE, PEC, measurement mitigation, dynamical decoupling, and circuit optimization.
Adapt mitigation choices as circuit behavior and noise change.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five paradigms and 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, APGEM reached 95.5% of oracle performance and significantly beat six fixed strategies; on noise models from eight IBM devices, it reached 99.9% of oracle utility at roughly 13,000 shots for 3–8 qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Results on device-derived noise models and 3–8-qubit systems do not establish performance on larger circuits or live hardware with drifting noise.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning

title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
authors: Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma
abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

infographic.key_insight: Loading classical data into a superconducting quantum computer has a substantial dynamic energy cost that depends on QRAM architecture, gate operation, and cryogenic attenuation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: At fixed target fidelity, optimizing operating conditions and attenuation across refrigerator stages can change average dynamic power by a factor of two or more.
method: Apply the metric-noise-resource framework to connect QRAM query fidelity and power with hardware parameters.
Analyze linear-depth multiplexer and bucket-brigade QRAM architectures, including thermal photons and gate errors.
Adapt bucket-brigade QRAM to native superconducting gates and refine fidelity estimates using the fully decomposed schedule.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a representative 12-address-qubit bucket-brigade query, the analysis yields 0.969 fidelity, 3.51×10⁻⁴ J dynamic energy, 4.38 W average dynamic power, and 64.4 W peak power.
infographic.watch_item: These are model-based dynamic-cost estimates, not a reported hardware demonstration or a complete accounting of system energy overheads.
infographic.paper_title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers

title: Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Giuseppe D'Ambruoso, Giovanni Gramegna, Domenico Pomarico, Giuseppe Magnifico, Cosmo Lupo
abstract: Many image classification tasks have labels that are unchanged by rotations and reflections. Equivariant quantum neural networks incorporate such symmetries by design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is difficult to isolate. Equivariant quantum circuits are usually compared with architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. Here, we investigate the role of invariance in a controlled setting, classifying images whose labels are invariant under the dihedral group $D_4$. We compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and number of trainable parameters, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, and benchmark invariant implementations against non-invariant ones in terms of generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning and resilience to a realistic noise model. On four binary tasks, including MNIST and two scientific data sets of galaxies and red blood cells, the invariant models trained on a few tens of images show better generalization than non-invariant ones. Invariance also makes the models immune to orientation shortcuts: when trained with a class-dependent corner watermark, the non-invariant models learn the watermark and often drop to chance level when it is moved. We show that the gain in accuracy of invariant models persists also under a realistic noise model.

infographic.key_insight: Building rotation and reflection invariance into quantum neural networks can reduce overfitting and prevent orientation-based shortcut learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For image tasks with symmetry-preserving labels, invariant quantum models can improve generalization from small training sets without increasing trainable parameter counts.
method: Compare four eight-qubit models on image labels invariant under the dihedral group D4.
Match encoding, circuit structure and parameter counts, with equivalent dynamical Lie algebras.
Test generalization, class-dependent corner-watermark shortcuts and realistic simulated noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four binary tasks, including MNIST, galaxies and red blood cells, invariant models generalized better from a few tens of training images, resisted orientation shortcuts and retained accuracy gains under noise.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover eight-qubit binary classifiers and a noise model; scalability and performance on physical quantum hardware remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks

title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
authors: Daniel Barter, Jacob C. Bridgeman, Chris Dawson, Terry Farrelly, Shane Fleming, Mercedes Gimeno-Segovia
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

infographic.key_insight: PRISM uses a transformer to decode erasure-dominated quantum errors, matching integer-programming decoders’ logical error rates while running significantly faster.
infographic.engineering_relevance: An optimized AMD VP1902 FPGA implementation demonstrates 6.59 µs latency and 1.56 µs amortized decoding time per logical block at distance 8 in space and time.
method: Exploit known erasure locations to decode combined Pauli and erasure errors.
Benchmark across surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes.
Optimize the decoder and FPGA implementation for low-latency inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks cover code distances up to 24 and error rates up to 50% of threshold, with logical error rates matching integer-programming-based decoders.
infographic.watch_item: The reported FPGA timing is for distance-8 blocks; comparable real-time performance at larger code distances remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time

title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
authors: Kunal Kumar, Kimberlee Keithley, Toshiya Iwamori, Shu Kanno, Ikko Hamamura, Takao Kobayashi
abstract: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits ($1.2 \times 10^8$ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)$_3$-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

infographic.key_insight: Transformer-based circuit generators trained with quantum-hardware feedback produced compact state-preparation circuits for molecular energy estimation at up to 70 qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-trained circuit generation could reduce two-qubit gate requirements for quantum chemistry workflows relevant to organotin photoresist modeling.
method: Train molecular-descriptor-conditioned generative quantum eigensolver policies first on a noiseless simulator, then on IBM Heron hardware.
Use generated circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization, with a reward penalty discouraging Hartree–Fock-only sampling.
Transfer policies to organotin hydroxides without retraining, then rank and recover cached measurement counts classically without further QPU calls.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 28 runs at 46–70 qubits, 27 achieved energies within 15 mHa of DMRG references (median error: 4.5 mHa); selected circuits at 56–70 qubits used 34–72× fewer two-qubit gates than device-transpiled LUCJ circuits.
infographic.watch_item: The four main training runs required 120 million shots, and classical reference energies informed training; these results do not establish end-to-end quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits

title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
authors: Edward Jiang, Timothy Heightman, Marcin Płodzień
abstract: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

infographic.key_insight: Normalizing flows can represent quantum gates as transformations between phase-space probability distributions, enabling a generative-model approach to classical quantum circuit simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a potential route to more accurate neural simulation of large quantum circuits on classical hardware.
method: Represent N-qubit states as probability distributions on a smooth 2N-dimensional manifold.
Parameterize unitary gates as normalizing flows between these distributions.
Learn phase-space representations of quantum circuits using generative models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on three common circuit families and higher accuracy than current state-of-the-art neural network methods at large system sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify runtime, memory requirements, or training costs, so practical scalability remains unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space

title: Analog quantum approximate optimization algorithm for solving the weighted MaxCut problem on three-dimensional single-atom Rydberg array
authors: Junxi Chen, I. I. Beterov
abstract: We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.

infographic.key_insight: Analog QAOA on a three-dimensional Rydberg-atom array uses complementary optimization strategies to outperform Goemans–Williamson rounding on nearly all tested weighted MaxCut instances in noiseless simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Encoding graph weights in interatomic interactions offers a hardware-oriented route to quantum optimization using global laser control and site-dependent detunings.
method: Choose 3D atom positions to encode problem weights in interaction energies.
Drive trapped Rydberg atoms with global laser pulses and site-dependent detunings.
Combine discretized quantum annealing and graph-neural-network warm starts in an optimization portfolio.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each, including sampling statistics, pulse-time costs, and quantum-trajectory emulation with a realistic Aquila error model.
infographic.watch_item: The reported advantage is noiseless and limited to small simulated benchmarks; noisy hardware performance and scalability remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Analog quantum approximate optimization algorithm for solving the weighted MaxCut problem on three-dimensional single-atom Rydberg array

title: Dynamical GKP codes
authors: Jonathan Pelletier, Baptiste Royer
abstract: Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

infographic.key_insight: Dynamical GKP codes extend measurement-driven quantum error correction to oscillator-based encodings using time-dependent phase-space translation measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The two-mode square–hexagonal Floquet construction reduces measurement weight while combining square and hexagonal logical gates, potentially simplifying implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group.
method: Formulate subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices.
Adapt ancestry, detector, and benign-error tools from dynamical qubit codes.
Compute syndrome and code distance using a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical framework illustrated by a two-mode Floquet code and shows that irrational symplectic-overlap measurements reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report hardware validation or performance under finite squeezing and realistic measurement noise.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamical GKP codes

title: Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition
authors: Matthew Brunet, Leah Prepchuk, Rebekah Herrman
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a near-term quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its accuracy and resource requirements may scale poorly with problem size or structure, reducing its utility in practice. Approaches such as the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) seek to address this by iteratively reducing an input problem until it reaches a size where it can be solved using QAOA while maintaining the same optimal solution. This algorithm, however, requires solving integer programs that have exponentially many variables, and can result in suboptimal solutions, as the integer programs may contain slack terms. In this work, we propose a heuristic called the Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) algorithm. Its novelty lies in its use of QAOA as a subroutine for sparsifying a graph through local vertex-merging. The algorithm, when used to sparsify MaxCut problems that are then solved using QAOA, achieves higher approximation ratios across all tested graphs than GDOA for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs. We then compare the time-to-solution and approximation ratio of QEGD to other QAOA variants a collection of Erdös-Rényi graphs. QEGD has higher approximation ratios on average than QAOA$^2$ and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs. It also results in higher average approximation ratios than DC-QAOA on sparse Erdös-Rényi graphs and comparable average approximation ratio on denser Erdös-Rényi graphs. However, its average wall-clock time is between 0.4\% and 5\% of the average DC-QAOA wall-clock time.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) uses QAOA-guided local vertex merging to simplify MaxCut graphs and improve solution quality in the reported tests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QEGD offers a way to reduce graph size before QAOA optimization, with reported average wall-clock times of 0.4%–5% of DC-QAOA’s.
method: Use QAOA as a subroutine to guide local vertex merging.
Sparsify the MaxCut graph through these merges.
Solve the reduced problem using QAOA.
infographic.evidence_signal: QEGD outperformed GDOA on tested random 5- and 6-regular graphs, exceeded QAOA² and ParaQAOA in average approximation ratio on tested Erdős–Rényi graphs, and beat DC-QAOA on sparse graphs while remaining comparable on denser ones.
infographic.watch_item: QEGD is a heuristic; the abstract does not establish optimality guarantees or performance on quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition

title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Seyong Lee, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

infographic.key_insight: The FTQC compiler preserves error-correction metadata in typed intermediate representations, making fault-tolerant quantum programs inspectable and retargetable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: An error-correction-aware pipeline helps engineers verify code-specific choices, estimate resource costs, and target simulators or quantum hardware.
method: Represent logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames as typed SSA values in an open-source MLIR dialect.
Use two-level lowering to target OpenQASM 3, QIR, Stim, and IQM hardware.
Analyze fault-tolerant resource requirements within the intermediate representation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Case studies span three code families: decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3× on ORNL’s 20-qubit Pathfinder, while a QFT-3 magic-state factory required 5× the encoded circuit’s peak qubits.
infographic.watch_item: The reported case studies do not establish scalability to large fault-tolerant workloads, where magic-state factories can impose substantial resource overhead.
infographic.paper_title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing

title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
authors: Masanori Hanada, Jiwoo Seo, Seok-Kyun Son, Junggi Yoon
abstract: Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks, where inter-register interactions prevent this exact compression, show that the preferred encoding depends on the grid size and the evolution time.

infographic.key_insight: Exactly compressed unary circuits resolve bosonic tunneling on IBM and IonQ hardware, while much deeper binary product-formula circuits fail to reproduce the transfer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Encoding and circuit compilation jointly determine hardware feasibility, so qubit savings must be weighed against two-qubit gate depth.
method: Compare binary and unary position-lattice encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors.
Implement binary kinetic evolution with a quantum Fourier transform and unary evolution with excitation-conserving exchange gates.
Exploit the single-degree-of-freedom free-fermion structure to compress unary dynamics exactly into fixed-size nearest-neighbor circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: With about 200 two-qubit gates, unary circuits reduce right-well probability from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ; binary circuits using several thousand gates do not reproduce the transfer.
infographic.watch_item: Unary encoding requires one qubit per lattice site, and inter-register interactions in coupled oscillators prevent this exact compression, making encoding choice dependent on grid size and evolution time.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors

title: Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms
authors: Ankit Khandelwal, Nirmal M R, Aaryav Mishra, Debasmita Bhoumik, Dhinakaran Vinayagamurthy, M Girish Chandra
abstract: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) requires the calculation of highly accurate electronic-structure energies and nuclear forces at every time step, which can quickly become computationally expensive. Sample-based quantum diagonalization offers a route to such calculations on quantum hardware, but its use in AIMD simulations has so far been limited to active spaces of about 20 qubits. In these spaces, exact diagonalization is tractable, and the quantum circuits are typically built from standard coupled-cluster amplitudes. Here, we introduce SqDRIFT-AIMD, which combines randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) with analytical nuclear gradients. With SqDRIFT-AIMD, we obtain more accurate ground-state energies than the conventional coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) driven AIMD simulation for the $40$-qubit active space. We apply SqDRIFT-AIMD to study the dynamics of proton transfer in the Zundel cation, using circuits executed on IBM Heron r3 quantum processors. SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the $40$-qubit double-well PES and stay within a few m$E_\text{h}$ of CCSD at 52 qubits. The $40$-qubit SqDRIFT-AIMD trajectory tracks the SHCI-driven proton transfer to within $1.33$ mÅ and exhibits excellent total energy conservation, with a standard deviation of only $0.245$ m$E_\text{h}$. These results extend quantum-centric AIMD to active spaces beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.

infographic.key_insight: SqDRIFT-AIMD combines sampling-based quantum diagonalization with analytical nuclear gradients to extend quantum-centric molecular dynamics beyond active spaces tractable by exact diagonalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach advances quantum-assisted prediction of molecular motion by improving electronic energies while maintaining accurate proton-transfer dynamics and stable total energy.
method: Use randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) to estimate ground-state electronic energies.
Combine SqDRIFT with analytical nuclear gradients to propagate molecular dynamics.
Execute quantum circuits on IBM Heron r3 processors to study proton transfer in the Zundel cation.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 40 qubits, SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the double-well potential, the trajectory tracks SHCI-driven proton transfer within 1.33 mÅ, and total-energy standard deviation is 0.245 mEh; at 52 qubits, energies remain within a few mEh of CCSD.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract demonstrates dynamics at 40 qubits and energy calculations at 52 qubits, but does not establish end-to-end computational advantage or scaling to larger molecular systems.
infographic.paper_title: Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms

title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Sanziana Stelea, Anthony Gandon, Francesco Tacchino, Jad C. Halimeh, Ivano Tavernelli
abstract: Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.

infographic.key_insight: A 63-qubit superconducting processor probes nonperturbative electric-flux string dynamics in a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gauge redundancy provides directly measurable constraints for error detection, helping quantum hardware access dynamics that challenge classical tensor-network simulations.
method: Evolve localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges and explicit magnetic plaquette interactions.
Measure spatial charge, flux, and string-path occupations to track spreading and transverse rearrangements.
Combine local Gauss-law constraints, 12 ancilla qubits, and noise rescaling.
infographic.evidence_signal: Circuits with up to 15 second-order Trotter steps reveal rapid spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced interior matter occupation near pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields.
infographic.watch_item: Finite circuit depth, Trotter approximation, and hardware noise constrain accessible evolution; the abstract does not establish a quantitative quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor

title: Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
authors: Soumya Sarkar, Rakshit Gharat, Nam Nguyen, Gavin Brennen
abstract: Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with $L$ cavities, $N$ emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff $n\_{\max}$, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary $L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil$-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with $16$ to $256$ cavities, the controlled walk uses $4.75$--$8.11%$ fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as $g^{(2)}(0)$. With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.

infographic.key_insight: An in-place photon-hopping circuit reduces logical resource costs for fault-tolerant quantum simulation of Tavis–Cummings lattices while supporting both closed- and open-system dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The resource estimates help assess fault-tolerant hardware requirements for simulating light–matter lattices, including state preparation and observable measurement.
method: Block-encode photon hopping and local light–matter exchange using ladder-operator circuits.
Use generalized quantum signal processing for closed-system evolution and retarded spectral-function estimation.
Use sampled first-order dilation for dissipative dynamics and transient photon-statistics estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three uniform-coefficient examples spanning 16–256 cavities, the controlled walk uses 4.75–8.11% fewer Toffoli gates than a matched two-register implementation and eliminates an auxiliary photon register.
infographic.watch_item: These are logical resource estimates rather than hardware demonstrations; total costs also depend on precision, state preparation, measurement, and open-system timesteps.
infographic.paper_title: Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers

title: Pool-free, residual-triggered ansatz growth for variational imaginary-time evolution: when a fixed operator order beats adaptive screening
authors: Yu-Hao Chen, Renata Wong
abstract: Adaptive variational algorithms such as ADAPT-VQE and AVQITE screen an operator pool at every growth step, and ADAPT-VQE also re-optimizes all parameters. We study a pool-free alternative for variational imaginary-time evolution (VITE). The layers are fixed in advance by nested commutators of the Hamiltonian, grouped by symmetry and particle number, and the next layer is appended when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold. On five non-integrable systems (the mixed-field Ising chain and tori, and stretched H$_4$), this dynamic VITE reaches a relative error of $10^{-4}$ with 1.6-5.4 times fewer circuits than the cheapest of six to eight adaptive variants, including single-Pauli-string and qubit-excitation pools and batched ADAPT-VQE. On the chain the advantage persists from 8 to 16 sites. Screening and re-optimization account for most of the adaptive methods' cost. On the spin models, a longitudinal-field scan shows that the advantage requires broken integrability, which makes adaptive screening expensive. The advantage is lost on transverse-field Ising models, at tight targets (relative error $10^{-6}$) and where the schedule front-loads weak layers.

infographic.key_insight: A fixed, residual-triggered ansatz schedule can outperform adaptive operator screening for variational imaginary-time evolution on non-integrable systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Avoiding repeated operator-pool screening and global parameter re-optimization can reduce circuit costs for ground-state estimation.
method: Predefine layers using nested Hamiltonian commutators, grouped by symmetry and particle number.
Append the next layer when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold.
Evolve parameters through variational imaginary-time updates without adaptive pool screening.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five non-integrable Ising and stretched-H₄ systems, the method reached 10⁻⁴ relative error using 1.6–5.4× fewer circuits than the cheapest adaptive comparator; the chain advantage persisted from 8 to 16 sites.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage disappears for transverse-field Ising models, at 10⁻⁶ relative-error targets, and when weak layers are scheduled too early.
infographic.paper_title: Pool-free, residual-triggered ansatz growth for variational imaginary-time evolution: when a fixed operator order beats adaptive screening

title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
authors: Sergio Hernández, Unai Aseguinolaza, David Aguirre, Marta Gili, Joseba Hernández, Guillermo Valverde
abstract: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

infographic.key_insight: Usable GHZ-state size can fall far below processor qubit count: the best superconducting devices passed at 27 and 24 qubits, while a 12-qubit trapped-ion device passed with its full register.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Application-specific cloud benchmarks can guide hardware selection more reliably than physical qubit counts or median calibration metrics alone.
method: Benchmarked nine cloud-accessible processors from five vendors across superconducting and trapped-ion technologies.
Used QuSquare multipartite entanglement tests and direct fidelity estimation with default compilation and no error mitigation.
Searched for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity was statistically compatible with the F = 1/2 entanglement threshold.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that tightening the criterion from threshold compatibility to certified genuine multipartite entanglement reduced devices succeeding at any tested size from nine to four.
infographic.watch_item: Threshold compatibility does not certify entanglement, and reported passing sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule.
infographic.paper_title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services

title: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits
authors: Jamal Slim
abstract: Quantum processors now measure qubits in the middle of a circuit, and the stream of outcomes is the raw output of error correction, measurement-based state preparation and monitored dynamics. For a scrambling circuit, predicting the statistics of this stream is as hard as simulating the processor, so there is no exact reference to check it against once the device outgrows classical simulation. We show that near the light cone the problem becomes exactly solvable, for any two-qubit gate. In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, measurements along the edge of the light cone form a two-state Markov chain, and measurements $d$ sites inside the edge are generated by $\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1$ qubits that move with it, while the rest of the chain, however large, acts on them as a memoryless bath. The memory of the record is therefore quantized, one bit on the edge and at most one more for every site of displacement, a bound that generic gates attain. The same causal structure determines which hardware noise the record can see, removes that sensitivity at no gate cost, and yields a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, a demonstration with its analysis specified in advance finds the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone, and none where the theory forbids it. This gives dynamic circuits an exact reference at any system size, and shows that the collision models of open-system theory arise exactly inside chaotic dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Near a quantum circuit’s light-cone edge, measurement records have exactly solvable, quantized memory despite otherwise complex scrambling dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides exact benchmarks for dynamic quantum circuits beyond classical simulation limits and identifies which hardware noise affects measurement records.
method: Analyze brickwork circuits with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background.
Map edge measurements to a two-state Markov chain.
Represent records d sites inside the edge using floor(d/2)+1 moving memory qubits coupled to a memoryless bath.
infographic.evidence_signal: A demonstration on a 156-qubit superconducting processor, with analysis specified in advance, found predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone and none where theory forbids it.
infographic.watch_item: Exact guarantees rely on the specified initialization, circuit geometry and measurement placement; they should not be assumed for arbitrary dynamic circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits

title: Frustration-free control for quantum-state preparation: an exact first-passage theory
authors: T. Dörstel, T. C. Lang, T. Iadecola, J. H. Wilson, M. Buchhold
abstract: Quantum circuits based on local measurements and feedback can autonomously prepare and stabilize entangled many-body states. In frustration-free control, the target manifold is specified by local constraints, whose violations are detected by measurement and removed by feedback. We develop an exact theory of this mechanism for the preparation of Dicke states of $N_q$ qubits. Dicke states span the permutation-symmetric subspace, one per magnetization sector. Local singlet projectors define the constraints and detect departures from permutation symmetry. The resulting dynamics closes exactly on the span of the $N_q(N_q-1)/2$ singlet-pair projectors and is equivalent to a classical first-passage process: measurements move the pair endpoints, while feedback absorbs pairs on measured bonds. The closure reduces the exponentially large many-body Liouvillian to a generator of polynomial size. In one dimension we solve this process in closed form. Its slowest rate, $2[1-\cos(π/N_q)]$ in units of the measurement rate, is an exact Liouvillian eigenvalue. For any scheme of this class, the relaxation time is bounded below by the inverse fraction of pair configurations on which feedback acts; local feedback reaches $O(N_q)$ of $O(N_q^2)$ configurations, requiring a time at least linear in $N_q$. A second exact closure determines the final state reached from any initial condition. Extensions to modified transport, restricted feedback, and physical errors yield an exact transport-to-absorber crossover, geometric preparation laws, and a bound on the stationary leakage. An exact second-moment closure determines the ensemble fluctuations: the measurement noise is conserving, while feedback generates removal shot noise and pair correlations. Preparation, acceleration, robustness, and fluctuations are thus governed by one exactly solvable process: the transport and absorption of local constraint violations.

infographic.key_insight: Preparing permutation-symmetric Dicke states via local measurements and feedback maps exactly to a classical first-passage process that transports and absorbs singlet-pair constraint violations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The mapping replaces exponentially large many-body dynamics with a polynomial-size generator for analyzing preparation speed, feedback geometry, robustness, and fluctuations.
method: Detect violations of permutation symmetry using local singlet projectors.
Close the dynamics exactly on N_q(N_q−1)/2 pair projectors, with measurements moving endpoints and feedback absorbing pairs.
Use additional exact closures to determine final states and ensemble fluctuations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results include the exact one-dimensional Liouvillian eigenvalue 2[1−cos(π/N_q)] in measurement-rate units and an at-least-linear relaxation-time bound for local feedback; the abstract reports no hardware evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Exact solvability does not imply fast preparation: the reported one-dimensional eigenvalue scales as N_q⁻², implying a quadratic slow relaxation timescale.
infographic.paper_title: Frustration-free control for quantum-state preparation: an exact first-passage theory

title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
authors: Zhihao Zhang, Shuaifan Cao, Xinyang Yu, Yanyan Chen, Yueyang Min, Yingzhou Li
abstract: Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays. In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the $10^{-4}$ level. We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of $1.43\%$ for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below $10^{-9}$ for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency. By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed dual-species atom-array architecture uses global driving and atom-mediated selectivity to enable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation without locally addressed quantum gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Replacing local gate addressing could reduce control complexity and associated calibration requirements in large-scale neutral-atom quantum processors.
method: Use interspecies Rydberg interactions to selectively control qubits under global driving.
Construct a universal native instruction set: Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL).
Compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, parallelizing operations to suppress crosstalk.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports crosstalk suppression to the 10^-4 level and, under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, a 1.43% quantum-memory threshold and cultivated magic-state logical error below 10^-9.
infographic.watch_item: The reported fault-tolerance performance is model-based; experimental validation must establish that global control and dual-species interactions sustain the assumed noise levels at scale.
infographic.paper_title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
